content: Home uterine activity monitoring is designed to detect an increase in uterine contraction frequency early, allowing for timely intervention with tocolytic medications to delay labor and extend pregnancy duration. However, its effectiveness in reducing preterm birth-related complications remains controversial. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether home uterine activity monitoring improves outcomes for women and their infants who are at high risk of preterm birth, compared to standard care without such monitoring. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group’s Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, covering publications up to June 28, 2016. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving home uterine activity monitoring, with or without patient education, were included. Data were independently assessed by two reviewers, and the quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Fifteen studies involving 6008 participants were included, with data contributed by 13 studies. Women using home uterine monitoring were less likely to deliver before 34 weeks of gestation (risk ratio [RR] 0.78, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.62 to 0.99; three studies, 1596 women; high-quality evidence). However, this finding was not consistent when the analysis was restricted to studies with a low risk of bias (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.00; one study, 1292 women). There was no significant difference in perinatal mortality rates between the groups (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.72; two studies, 2589 babies; low-quality evidence). Similarly, no difference was observed in the rate of preterm births before 37 weeks (average RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.01; eight studies, 4834 women; very low-quality evidence). Infants born to women using home uterine monitoring were less likely to be admitted to neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) (average RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.96; five studies, 2367 babies; moderate-quality evidence). However, this benefit was not observed when the analysis was limited to studies with a low risk of bias (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.01; one study, 1292 babies). Women using home uterine monitoring had more unscheduled antenatal visits (mean difference [MD] 0.48, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.64; two studies, 1994 women; moderate-quality evidence). They were also more likely to receive prophylactic tocolytic therapy (average RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.45; seven studies, 4316 women; moderate-quality evidence). However, this difference was not evident when the analysis was restricted to studies with a low risk of bias (average RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.65; three studies, 3749 women; low-quality evidence). The number of antenatal hospital admissions did not differ significantly between women using home uterine monitoring and those receiving standard care (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.11; three studies, 1494 women; low-quality evidence). No data were available on maternal anxiety or the acceptability of home uterine monitoring. In conclusion, home uterine monitoring may reduce NICU admissions but is associated with an increase in unscheduled antenatal visits and tocolytic treatment. The overall quality of evidence is low to moderate, and sensitivity analyses limited to low-bias studies did not show significant group differences. There is no evidence of an impact on maternal or perinatal outcomes, such as perinatal mortality or the incidence of preterm birth.
